data.title: Blockstream Researchers Publish Security Analysis of SHRINCS Bitcoin Signature Scheme

data.title: Congress Passes Bill to Protect Older Investors From Financial Fraud
data.description: According to CNBC, Congress approved the bipartisan Financial Exploitation Prevention Act of 2025, sending H.R. 2478 to President Donald Trump after the Senate passed it by unanimous consent Wednesday night. The House passed the measure in June. It would allow mutual fund companies and transfer agents to delay redemption payments for up to 15 business days when they reasonably suspect financial exploitation, with a possible 10-business-day extension and further extensions by regulators, government agencies or courts. The protections would cover investors age 65 and older and younger adults with certain mental or physical impairments. Companies opting in would have to ask customers for at least one trusted contact. Adults age 60 or older reported losing about $3 billion to fraud in 2025, up 25% from $2.4 billion in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

data.title: Experts Say Ron Johnson's 'Ponzi Scheme' Label Misstates Social Security
data.description: According to CNBC, Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson called Social Security “a legal Ponzi scheme” at a Wednesday hearing, but experts said the comparison overlooks how the program works. Benefits are funded mainly by payroll taxes, and Social Security cannot borrow. Johnson said his earlier comments were imprecise and proposed legislation allowing general revenues to fund retirement benefits after the trust fund reaches insolvency. Social Security trustees project the retirement trust fund could run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, when 78% of scheduled benefits would be payable; the combined retirement and disability funds could be depleted in the third quarter of 2034, when 83% would be payable.

data.title: Chicago Fed President Austan D. Goolsbee Says AI Buildout and Spending Could Overheat Economy
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, Chicago Fed President Austan D. Goolsbee said he was concerned that AI-related construction could overheat the economy. He said the Federal Reserve’s task of preventing that outcome was becoming more complicated.

Goolsbee said data center construction, corporate investment and consumer spending based on expectations of future wealth could contribute to overheating. He called inflation the biggest problem facing the U.S. economy and said he was concerned that tariff-driven inflation was showing greater persistence.

He added that he saw no signs of stagflation. Hiring had declined, but the labor market remained stable.
